paragraphs: Rav Adda bar Matna or Matnah.[^1]

None of the writers on the amoraim noticed that there were two men bearing this name: one was a disciple of Rav and was always called “bar Matnah,” while the other, a disciple of Rava, was called “bar Matna.” Only through copyists’ errors was Matnah sometimes written in place of Matna, or the reverse. Rav Adda bar Matna, spelled with an alef, was a great disciple of Abaye and Rava. He asked Abaye questions in Shabbat 48a and 94a and Kiddushin 64b; raised objections to Abaye in Bava Metzia 12a and Bava Batra 86a; and addressed Abaye as “Master” in Ketubot 77b.

So too with Rava: Chullin 77a relates that a case of a broken bone came before Abaye, who held it over for three pilgrimage festivals. Rav Adda bar Matna told him, “Go before Rava son of Rav Yosef bar Chama, for his knife is sharp.”[^2] We likewise find him putting a contradiction to Rava in Eruvin 34b and raising objections to him in Shabbat 8a; Eruvin 8b and 34b; Ketubot 28a; Gittin 28b; and Bava Metzia 12a. He and Ravina asked Rava a question in Berakhot 23a.

Nevertheless, he was undoubtedly older than Ravina, since Rav Adda bar Matna had also merited to see Rav Yosef and receive teachings from him. Thus, in Pesachim 13a he says to Rav Yosef, “You expressly told us”; and Niddah 25b has “Rav Adda [bar Matna] said in the name of Rav Yosef.” Yet both he and Ravina sat before Rava. This explains Bava Metzia 12a: “Rav Pappa said to Rava”; some say it was Rav Adda bar Matna who said it to Rava, and some say Ravina. All three were Rava’s disciples, and there was uncertainty as to which of them had asked Rava. In Ketubot 85a, Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Matna were sitting before Rava.

In Shevuot 18a and Zevachim 100b, Rav Adda bar Matna raised an objection to Rava. Ravina spoke to Rav Adda bar Matna, and Rava said, “Heed what your teacher says.” Rashi explains that “your teacher” refers to Ravina. This is indeed puzzling, for Ravina was not his teacher. It is very likely that this is a gloss by a mistaken student that entered Rashi’s commentary. The straightforward meaning is that Rava was speaking about himself: he should heed Rava.

Dikdukei Soferim, at that passage in Shevuot, cites the Rashba’s novellae with the reading that Ravina told him, “Heed what your teacher says.” This too is difficult, since Rava was also Ravina’s teacher: why did he say “your teacher”? Perhaps the reading should be “רבנן.”[^3]

In Menachot 43a we find Rav Adda before Rava, reporting in the name of Rav Avira. Perhaps this should read Rav Adda bar Matna, or, following the reading in Dikdukei Soferim, Rav Acha. The wording in Menachot 59b, “Rav Adda said: Rav Ashi’s view is reasonable,” is a scribal error. It should read as in Zevachim 34b: “Rav Shayya said: Rav Ashi’s view,” etc.

In Yoma 37a, “Rav Shmuel b. P. explained it before Rav Adda,” the reading in Dikdukei Soferim is correct: it should read “Rav Shmuel bar Acha explained it before Rav Pappa.” Likewise, Sanhedrin 108b has “Rav Adda said; they say in the school of R' Shila”; there the Arukh’s reading is “Rav and R' Shila.” This removes all of Seder HaDorot’s difficulties about the identity of an unspecified Rav Adda.[^4]

In Niddah 67b, Rav Adda said to Rav Chinana of Sura, “Was this not what happened with the wife of Abba Mari the exilarch? She became angry, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak went to appease her.” In Beit Vaad laChakhamim, the gaon who authored Melo HaRo’im suggests that Rav Adda was Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak’s brother-in-law: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak was the exilarch’s son-in-law, and Rav Adda was his son. He understood “Abba Mari” as “my father, my teacher.” With all respect, this is a mistake: (a) it was not Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak who was the nasi’s son-in-law, but Rav Nachman bar Yaakov who was a son-in-law of the exilarch’s household; (b) Abba Mari was the exilarch’s actual name.

It is very likely that this man was Rav Adda bar Matna. Eruvin 22b relates that Rav Adda bar Matna studied Torah amid the greatest hardship, for it is related that when he went to the study house, his wife asked, “What shall I do with your children?” He replied, “Have the marsh plants run out?” When Rava heard this remarkable incident, he applied to him the verse “black as a raven”: it refers to one who makes himself as cruel to his children as a raven.

Rav Adda bar Matnah, however, was a disciple of Rav and transmitted teachings in his name, as in Shabbat 118b, Yoma 4b and Avodah Zarah 28b. Berakhot 30b mistakenly has “Rabbah said”; it should read “Rav said.” He was something of a peer of Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet. Thus Ketubot 5b has Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet sitting, with Rav Adda bar Matnah sitting beside them, debating with them and raising an objection to them.

He is also mentioned in Beitzah 17b. In Shabbat 140a, Rav Acha bar Yosef suffered from heaviness of the heart and came before Mar Ukva. He told him, “Go and ask in the study house.” He was told, “The school of Rav Adda taught”—some say, “the school of Mar bar Rav Adda.” Perhaps this was bar Matnah.

notes.text: Matna represents מתנא, with a final alef; Matnah represents מתנה, with a final he. The distinction between two men is Hyman’s argument here.
The sharp knife is an image of Rava’s acuity in deciding the case.
The printed proposed reading רבנן usually means “the rabbis”; Hyman’s argument here concerns their shared teacher, in contrast to “your teacher” (רבך).
Hyman abbreviates the first patronymic as ב״פ; his proposed replacement gives bar Acha in full. Rav Shayya follows the printed name שייא.
